question.text:
\[ \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ a & b & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

The covariance matrix $\Sigma$ for some random variables $X_1, X_2,$ and $X_3$ is given above. Find $a + b.$
question.explanation:
For random variables $X_1, \ldots, X_n,$ the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ is given by

\[ \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Var}[X_1] & \textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_2] & \cdots & \textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_n] \\ \textrm{Cov}[X_2,X_1] & \textrm{Var}[X_2] & \cdots & \textrm{Cov}[X_2,X_n] \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \textrm{Cov}[X_n,X_1] & \textrm{Cov}[X_n,X_2] & \cdots & \textrm{Var}[X_n] \end{bmatrix}. \]

That is,

  • the $i$th diagonal element is $\Sigma_{ii} = \textrm{Var}[X_i],$ and

  • the element in the $i$th row and $j$th column for $i \neq j$ is $\Sigma_{ij} = \textrm{Cov}[X_i, X_j].$

Now, note that \[ \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{Cov}[Y,X]. \] As a result, the covariance matrix is always symmetric (moreover, it is a positive semi-definite matrix).

So, we can find the missing elements as follows:

  • $a = \Sigma_{31} = \textrm{Cov}[X_3,X_1] = \textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_3] = \Sigma_{13} = 0$

  • $b = \Sigma_{32} = \textrm{Cov}[X_3,X_2] = \textrm{Cov}[X_2,X_3] = \Sigma_{23} = 2$

Therefore, $a + b = 0 +2 = 2.$

question.text: Consider two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with expectations $\textrm{E}[X] = 2,$ $\textrm{E}[Y] = 4,$ mixed moment $\textrm{E}[XY] = 10,$ and second raw moments $\textrm{E}[X^2] = 9$ and $\textrm{E}[Y^2] = 20.$ Find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
question.explanation:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ is given by

\[ \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Var}[X] & \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \textrm{Cov}[Y,X] & \textrm{Var}[Y] \end{bmatrix}. \]

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

\[ \textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2, \]

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

\[ \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y]. \]

First, let's find $\textrm{Var}[X]{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{Var}[X] &= \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2 \\[3pt] &= 9 - 2^2 \\[3pt] &= 5. \end{align}

Similarly,

\begin{align} \textrm{Var}[Y] &= \textrm{E}[Y^2] - \textrm{E}[Y]^2 \\[5pt] &= 20 - 4^2 \\[5pt] &= 4. \end{align}

Now lets find $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[3pt] &= 10 - 2 \cdot 4 \\[3pt] &= 2. \end{align}

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

\[ \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Var}[X] & \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \textrm{Cov}[Y,X] & \textrm{Var}[Y] \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

$f_Y$ $0.6$ $0.4$ $1$

Therefore, \begin{align} \textrm{Var}[Y] & = \textrm{E}[Y^2] - \textrm{E}[Y]^2 \\[5pt] & = 2.2 - 1.4^2 \\[5pt] & = 0.24. \end{align}

Finally, let's find $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\textrm{E}[XY]{:}$ \begin{align} \textrm{E}[XY] & = \sum\limits_{(x,y) \in S} xy \cdot f(x,y) \\[5pt] & = (2)(1)f(2,1) + (3)(1)f(3,1) + (2)(2)f(2,2) + (3)(2)f(3,2) \\[5pt] & = 2 \cdot 0.55 + 3 \cdot 0.05 + 4 \cdot 0.25 + 6 \cdot 0.15 \\[5pt] & = 3.15. \end{align}

question.text:

For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ is given by

\[ \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Var}[X] & \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \textrm{Cov}[Y,X] & \textrm{Var}[Y] \end{bmatrix}. \]

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

\[ \textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2, \]

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

\[ \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y]. \]

First, we find $\textrm{Var}[X].$ Using the given results, we have

\begin{align} \textrm{Var}[X] &= \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2 \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3} - \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^2 \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{2}{75}. \end{align}

Similarly, we compute $\textrm{E}[Y^2]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

\begin{align} \textrm{E}[Y^2] &= \int_0^1 \int_0^{x/2} y^2 \cdot f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}y \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \int_0^{x/2} 48y^3 (x-y) \, \textrm{d}y \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 48\int_0^1 \int_0^{x/2} \left( xy^3 - y^4 \right) \textrm{d}y \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 48\int_0^1 \left[ \dfrac1{4}xy^4 - \dfrac{1}{5}y^5 \right]_{y=0}^{y=x/2} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=48 \int_0^1 \left( \dfrac1{64}x^5 -\dfrac1{160}x^5 \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=48\cdot \dfrac3{320} \int_0^1 x^5 \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac9{20}\left[ \dfrac1{6} x^6 \right]_0^1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{40}. \end{align}

Therefore,

\begin{align} \textrm{Var}[Y] &= \textrm{E}[Y^2] - \textrm{E}[Y]^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{40} - \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{80}. \end{align}

\begin{align} \textrm{E}[XY] &= \int_0^1 \int_0^{x/2} xy \cdot f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}y \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \int_0^{x/2} 48xy^2(x-y) \, \textrm{d}y \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=48 \int_0^1 \int_0^{x/2} \left( x^2y^2 - xy^3 \right) \textrm{d}y \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 48\int_0^1 \left[ \dfrac13x^2y^3 - \dfrac14xy^4 \right]_{y=0}^{y=x/2} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 48\int_0^1 \left( \dfrac1{24}x^5 - \dfrac1{64}x^5 \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 48\cdot \dfrac5{192}\int_0^1 x^5 \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac5{4} \left[ \dfrac1{6}x^6 \right]_0^1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac5{24}. \end{align}

\begin{align} \textrm{Var}[Y] &= \textrm{E}[Y^2] - \textrm{E}[Y]^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{40}{27} - \left(\dfrac{20}{21}\right)^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{760}{1\,323}. \end{align}

Finally, let's find $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\textrm{E}[XY]{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{E}[XY] &= \int_0^2 \int_0^{x^2} xy \cdot f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}y \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^2 \int_0^{x^2} \dfrac{5}{16}xy (x^2-y) \, \textrm{d}y\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{16} \int_0^2 \int_0^{x^2} \left( x^3 y - xy^2 \right) \textrm{d}y \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{16} \int_0^2 \left[ \dfrac12y^2x^3 - \dfrac13y^3x \right]_{y=0}^{y=x^2} \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{16} \int_0^2 \left( \dfrac16x^7 \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{96} \int_0^2 x^7 \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{96} \left[ \dfrac1{8}x^8 \right]_0^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac53. \end{align}

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[3pt] &= \dfrac53 - \left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{20}{21}\right) \\[3pt] &=\dfrac{5}{63}. \end{align}

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

\[ \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Var}[X] & \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \textrm{Cov}[Y,X] & \textrm{Var}[Y] \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{5}{63} & \dfrac{5}{63} \\ \dfrac{5}{63} & \dfrac{760}{1\,323} \end{bmatrix} . \]

question.text:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

\[ f(x,y) = \begin{cases} x+y, \qquad & 0 \leq x \leq 1, \,\, 0 \leq y \leq 1, \\[5pt] 0, \qquad & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

Given that $\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[Y] = \dfrac{7}{12},$ and $E[X^2]=\dfrac{5}{12},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
question.explanation:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ is given by

\[ \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Var}[X] & \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \textrm{Cov}[Y,X] & \textrm{Var}[Y] \end{bmatrix}. \]

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

\[ \textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2, \]

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

\[ \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y]. \]

First, we find $\textrm{Var}[X].$ Using the given results, we have

\begin{align} \textrm{Var}[X] &= \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2 \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{5}{12} - \left(\dfrac{7}{12}\right)^2 \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{11}{144}. \end{align}

Similarly, we compute $\textrm{E}[Y^2]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

\begin{align} \textrm{E}[Y^2] &= \int_0^1 \int_0^1 y^2 \cdot f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \int_0^1 y^2 (x+y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \int_0^1 \left( xy^2 + y^3 \right) \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \left[ \dfrac12x^2y^2 + xy^3 \right]_{x=0}^{x=1} \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \left( \dfrac12y^2 + y^3 \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac16y^3 + \dfrac14y^4 \right]_0^1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac16 + \dfrac14 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{12}. \end{align}

Therefore,

\begin{align} \textrm{Var}[Y] &= \textrm{E}[Y^2] - \textrm{E}[Y]^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{12} - \left(\dfrac{7}{12}\right)^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{11}{144}. \end{align}

Finally, let's find $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\textrm{E}[XY]{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{E}[XY] &= \int_0^1 \int_0^1 xy \cdot f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \int_0^1 xy (x+y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \int_0^1 \left( x^2y + xy^2 \right) \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \left[ \dfrac13x^3y + \dfrac12x^2y^2 \right]_0^1 \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \left( \dfrac13y + \dfrac12y^2 \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac16y^2 + \dfrac16y^3 \right]_0^1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac16 + \dfrac16 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac13. \end{align}

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[3pt] &= \dfrac13 - \left(\dfrac{7}{12}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{7}{12}\right) \\[3pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{144}. \end{align}

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

\[ \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \textrm{Var}[X] & \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \textrm{Cov}[Y,X] & \textrm{Var}[Y] \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{11}{144} & -\dfrac{1}{144} \\ -\dfrac{1}{144} & \dfrac{11}{144} \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{144} \begin{bmatrix} 11 & -1 \\ -1 & 11 \end{bmatrix}. \]
